clue.text: Time for one's oats?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for a prison sentence
second meaning: the breakfast dish one makes from oats

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, doing porridge means serving time in prison; the other sense is the oatmeal breakfast. 'for' just links the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for a jail term and also the ordinary name of boiled oatmeal eaten at breakfast.

clue.text: Roman Catholic Father's "tired and emotional", we hear

parts.note: Pa is an informal word for father; the 's is 'is'

indicators.note: we hear tells us the spoken words stand in for a written word that sounds the same

parts.note: a jokey British euphemism for drunk, i.e. pissed

explanation.surface: A priest is said to be drunk, according to gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tired and emotional' is a well-known British press euphemism for drunk; 'pissed' is British slang for drunk. Said together, 'Pa pissed' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A papist is a derogatory term for a member of the Roman Catholic Church, loyal to the Pope.

clue.text: Joint has umpire ever on the up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a referee, shortened to ref
e'er, the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A cannabis cigarette is always getting more popular with the match official.
explanation.definitionFit: A reefer is a slang term for a cannabis cigarette, which is also called a joint.

clue.text: It may be covered in black around the old city

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the black word goes around the city name, holding it inside

parts.note: sable is the heraldic term for black
Ur was an ancient Mesopotamian city

explanation.surface: Something might be wrapped in dark cloth round an ancient town.
explanation.walkthrough: Sable is black in heraldry; Ur, a Sumerian city, is a crossword favourite. 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something insurable is a risk an insurer is willing to cover with a policy.

clue.text: Spirit (whiskey) moving triers to be authors, albeit unacclaimed

parts.note: a ghost is a spirit
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: moving suggests the letters of triers are shifted about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker's spirit makes people who try hard become writers without credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whiskey' with an e is the NATO alphabet's word for W, not a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghostwriters write books or speeches published under another person's name, so they get no public credit.

clue.text: Mark, the sailor, is a divine six-footer!

parts.note: a scar is a mark left on the skin
AB, able-bodied seaman

explanation.surface: A seaman called Mark is described as a heavenly tall man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it means an insect with six legs; the scarab beetle was sacred in ancient Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarab is a beetle, an insect with six legs, which ancient Egyptians revered as sacred.

clue.text: High point was a century break

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a rest is a break

explanation.surface: A cricketer's best moment was a hundred-run innings at the crease.
explanation.definitionFit: A crest is the top of a hill or wave, its peak.

clue.text: Sort of government for fogey outside drinking hole

indicators.note: the fogey word sits outside, wrapped around the drinking word

parts.note: an old fogey can be called a relic
a pub, informally a watering hole

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned type standing outside a bar sets out a political system.
explanation.definitionFit: A republic is a state run without a monarch, by elected representatives.

clue.text: Boring piece on birds (wading birds)

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: a drill bit bores holes
terns are seabirds

explanation.surface: A dull item about birds, specifically waders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like 'dull', but it means drilling.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitterns are marsh-dwelling herons that wade in reed beds.

clue.text: Recruit men to take on case from journalists' viewpoint

indicators.note: the first piece takes on the second, adding it after itself

parts.note: to press men is to force them into service, as a press gang did
a box is a case

explanation.surface: Enlist people to handle a legal case, from the reporters' angle.
explanation.definitionFit: A press box is the reserved seating area from which reporters watch a sports event.

clue.text: Tyrannical boss puts Lynham out to grass?

parts.note: Des Lynam is a British sports broadcaster (the clue misspells his surname)
both are slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A harsh manager forces a veteran TV presenter into retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: Des Lynam fronted BBC sports coverage for decades. 'Out to grass' suggests retirement, but grass and pot are both cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is an absolute ruler who uses power cruelly, a tyrant.

clue.text: Soldier takes leave in sensitive area

parts.note: a private is the lowest-ranked soldier
someone who takes leave parts, departing

explanation.surface: A soldier goes off on leave into a delicate region.
explanation.definitionFit: Private parts is a coy euphemism for the genitals, a sensitive part of the body.

clue.text: Lawrence's hesitation after introduction to Sandra Bullock

indicators.note: the Lawrence pieces come after the opening letter
the introduction to a word is its opening letter

parts.note: only the opening letter of the name is used
T.E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia
er, the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: An actor pauses after being introduced to the film star Sandra Bullock.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandra Bullock is the actress, but here 'Bullock' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A steer is a young castrated male ox raised for beef, which is also called a bullock.

clue.text: Record-holder to go by the board?

parts.note: your go in a game is your turn
a table is a board

explanation.surface: Somebody holding a record has been sidelined.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'go by the board' means be abandoned, which hides the split into a game move and a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A turntable is the rotating platform of a record player on which the vinyl disc sits.

clue.text: Britain above (anag)

indicators.note: the clue's own label tells us to rearrange the two words before it

parts.note: the two words are taken as written, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A bare crossword instruction to rearrange two words.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that 'anag' is itself a shortened word, an example of what the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: 'anag' is a shortened form of anagram, so it illustrates a shortened word form.

clue.text: Pain's relative to personal adviser

parts.note: agony is great pain
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: Suffering is linked to someone who gives private counsel.
explanation.walkthrough: An agony aunt is a British term for a newspaper advice columnist.
explanation.definitionFit: An agony aunt answers readers' letters about their private problems in a newspaper column.

clue.text: It's an earthly balance — so says IT organisation

indicators.note: organisation is arranging, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the three words are taken as written, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A geology term is defined, so a computer company says.
explanation.definitionFit: Isostasy is the gravitational equilibrium of the Earth's crust floating on the denser mantle.

clue.text: Travelling salesmen with no identification

indicators.note: travelling sets the letters in motion into a different order

parts.note: the word is taken as written, letter for letter

explanation.surface: Travelling salesmen go about without ID.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nameless is unnamed or anonymous, without any label.

clue.text: Manned satellite room at Waterloo?

parts.note: space is room
Waterloo is a London railway station, an example of a station

explanation.surface: A crewed spacecraft is likened to a room at a London terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: Waterloo is a major railway station in London; the question mark marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A space station is a large crewed spacecraft that orbits the Earth for long missions.

clue.text: One in trim is right to be more nervous

indicators.note: the one goes in the trim word

parts.note: an edge is a trim or border
I, the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone tidying a hedge is right to be more jittery.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgier means more tense and jumpy, more on edge.

clue.text: Minister for 150 at Morecambe?

parts.note: CL is 150 in Roman numerals
Eric Morecambe was a much-loved British comedian

explanation.surface: A government minister in charge of 150 seats at Morecambe, a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe is a Lancashire resort, but here it is Eric Morecambe of the comedy duo Morecambe and Wise.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister is a member of the clergy, a priest or pastor, as is a cleric.

clue.text: Potential driving hazard caused by amphetamines and gin?

parts.note: speed is slang for amphetamines
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: Drug and drink driving could be dangerous on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' here is a gin trap, a hunting snare, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A speed trap is a stretch of road where police catch speeding motorists, a risk to the driver.

clue.text: Escape to Kansas City?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to evade or escape
second meaning: ... City, a town in Kansas

explanation.walkthrough: Dodge City is the Wild West town in Kansas; the question mark flags that the answer is only part of its name. 'to' links.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodge is to evade, and Dodge City is a famous frontier town in Kansas.

clue.text: Greeting Trotter with a song

parts.note: yo is an informal greeting
Del Boy Trotter, the market trader in the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses

explanation.surface: Welcoming a runner with music.
explanation.walkthrough: Del Boy Trotter is the wheeler-dealer hero of the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A yodel is a type of Alpine singing that flips rapidly between chest voice and falsetto.

clue.text: It may be hidden by fag end ash

indicators.note: the answer is held by, inside, these words

parts.note: the answer runs across these words: letters 2-7 of 'fag end ash'

explanation.surface: Something could be concealed under cigarette ash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hidden' does double duty: it fits the definition and tells you the answer sits in the words. A fag is British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden agenda is a secret plan, so this kind of plan may be concealed.

clue.text: One dealing with "Our Price", perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters could form another word

parts.note: the shop's name is taken as written, letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone works for the record-shop chain Our Price.
explanation.walkthrough: Our Price was a British chain of record shops.
explanation.definitionFit: A croupier deals cards and runs the table in a casino.

clue.text: Middle East republic harbouring Sweden's sycophants

indicators.note: the republic harbours the letter for Sweden inside it

parts.note: Yemen is a republic in the Arabian peninsula
S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: An Arab nation shelters Swedish flatterers.
explanation.definitionFit: Yes men are people who always agree with a superior to please them, flatterers.

clue.text: Occult coteries looking silly

indicators.note: the letters look silly because they are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the word is taken as written, letter for letter

explanation.surface: Secret groups seem foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric means understood only by a small circle of initiates, hidden or mystical knowledge.
